safety_note: The prescribed dose, treatment decision and local urgent-contact plan take priority. Call 112 or 999 for severe breathing difficulty, severe chest pain, collapse, a new seizure, sudden weakness or speech difficulty, or uncontrolled bleeding. Follow your oncology unit’s written urgent-contact plan for other new or worsening symptoms; do not wait for the next appointment.

title: Dabrafenib alone — advanced melanoma
purpose: To control advanced BRAF V600-mutated melanoma using dabrafenib alone, with regular review of benefit, fever and other side effects.
schedule_summary: Dabrafenib twice daily, about 12 hours apart, every day. Take it on an empty stomach; there is no planned tablet-free week.
scope_note: This is dabrafenib monotherapy for advanced melanoma. Do not import the food, heart-testing, fertility or duration instructions of a different BRAF/MEK combination. The NCCP fever table states 38.5°C, while current EMA product information states interruption at 38°C for monotherapy; this guide uses the earlier current-product safety trigger and the team must reconcile the written plan.
indication_text: Adults with unresectable or metastatic melanoma and a confirmed BRAF V600 tumour mutation.
phases_note: Dabrafenib twice daily, about 12 hours apart, every day. Take it on an empty stomach; there is no planned tablet-free week.
timeline_note: This is a reference schedule. Your prescribed dose, blood results, symptoms and the team’s written plan determine whether treatment goes ahead.
consent_support: Discuss the exact diagnosis and treatment intent, expected benefit and uncertainty, alternatives, regimen-specific risks, tests, fertility, practical burdens and your preferences. This guide supports the consent conversation and does not replace it. This is dabrafenib monotherapy for advanced melanoma. Do not import the food, heart-testing, fertility or duration instructions of a different BRAF/MEK combination. The NCCP fever table states 38.5°C, while current EMA product information states interruption at 38°C for monotherapy; this guide uses the earlier current-product safety trigger and the team must reconcile the written plan.
urgent_extra: If your temperature is 38°C or higher, stop dabrafenib and contact the oncology team immediately under the current product information; do not restart on your own. Also call for shaking chills, dizziness, reduced urine, severe abdominal pain, eye pain or changed vision, or a blistering or spreading rash. Infection and medicine-related fever both need consideration.

agents.name: Dabrafenib
agents.explanation: Dabrafenib inhibits the altered BRAF V600 protein involved in melanoma growth. This guide describes dabrafenib alone for advanced melanoma. It does not include a second targeted medicine or a postoperative one-year treatment schedule.
agents.watch: A temperature of 38°C or higher requires immediate contact and interruption under the current product information; follow the written plan and do not restart without team advice.
risks: Skin changes and new skin cancers
Abdominal pain, pancreatic or kidney problems

passport_visit_note: Record the dose actually taken or administered, symptoms, tests and agreed next step. A planned or held visit is not a completed treatment dose.
anatomy: Fever, chills and headache can occur. At 38°C or higher, stop and call under the current product information; severe weakness, dizziness or confusion is urgent.
Pain, redness, light sensitivity or blurred vision may be inflammation. Prompt eye assessment may be needed.
Rash, thickened skin and new skin cancers can occur. Report a changing lesion, a persistent sore or severe rash.
Routine blood tests look for liver changes. Yellow skin or eyes or dark urine need prompt review.
Fever, vomiting or diarrhoea can cause dehydration and kidney injury. Report reduced urine or inability to drink.
Nausea and bowel changes can occur. Severe or persistent abdominal pain needs urgent assessment because pancreatic inflammation is possible.
Joint pain, muscle pain or fatigue may affect activity. Report increasing pain or weakness and ask about suitable relief.
Sore thickened skin or redness on palms and soles can affect walking and grip. Report it early and ask for skin care tailored to your symptoms.

chronology_notes.title: Schedule and review
chronology_notes.text: Dabrafenib twice daily, about 12 hours apart, every day. Take it on an empty stomach; there is no planned tablet-free week.

chronology_notes.title: Holds, missed treatment and phase changes
chronology_notes.text: Skip a missed dose if the next dose is due in less than six hours. Do not take two doses together to make up for it. If you vomit after a dose, do not take a replacement dose; take the next dose when due. The team must give instructions for restarting after fever or another treatment hold.

administration_text: The usual starting dose is 150 mg twice daily, about 12 hours apart. Take capsules at least one hour before or at least two hours after food. Swallow whole with water. Use the prescribed strength and dose, and check the label again after any interruption or dose change.
monitoring_summary: Confirm BRAF V600 and check blood count, kidney and liver function, ECG, medicines and skin. Record existing skin lesions and relevant head-and-neck or other cancer assessments so later changes can be compared. Monthly blood count, kidney and liver tests, and monthly skin review. Repeat ECG when clinically indicated. NCCP also describes head-and-neck review every three months and other surveillance according to the individual assessment; this is separate from the cancer-response scan plan. Continue skin surveillance for up to six months after stopping, as specified by NCCP. Keep the agreed review for other new lesions and the individual response-imaging plan. No fixed tumour-marker schedule is assumed.

support.title: Supportive medicines and symptom plan
support.text: NCCP classifies dabrafenib as minimal-to-low emetogenic risk; anti-sickness treatment follows local and individual need. Agree a written fever plan and keep a thermometer and actual urgent-contact number. The team may prescribe fever treatment and hydration advice after assessment; fever medicine is not a substitute for contacting them. Anti-sickness treatment is selected individually.

support.title: Skin and daily care
support.text: Inspect skin and report new lumps, persistent warty growths, sores or changing moles. Report painful thickening or redness of palms and soles before it limits walking or hand use. Protect skin from the sun and attend monthly skin reviews.

support.title: Fertility, pregnancy and breastfeeding
support.text: Use effective contraception during dabrafenib alone and for two weeks after the last dose. Hormonal contraception may be less reliable; agree an effective alternative. A longer interval applies if another medicine requires it, so use your actual prescribed plan. Discuss fertility and breastfeeding before treatment.

evidence.title: What the treatment evidence can and cannot tell you
evidence.intro: Evidence needs to match the medicine, dose combination, disease stage and previous treatment.
evidence.population: 250 previously untreated patients with unresectable stage III or stage IV BRAF V600E melanoma
evidence.interpretation: Median progression-free survival was 5.1 versus 2.7 months; hazard ratio 0.30, 95% CI 0.18–0.51. These are group results from that study, not a prediction for you.
limitations: Advanced-disease monotherapy evidence, not postoperative dabrafenib/trametinib evidence.
The comparator and treatment era do not establish superiority over current combinations.
Personal benefit depends on the cancer, previous treatment, general health and the available alternatives.

chapters.title: Understanding your diagnosis and treatment goal
chapters.intro: Use your own pathology, stage and agreed plan alongside this guide.

items.title: Your diagnosis and stage
items.text: Keep the pathology report, original melanoma site, stage and known sites of spread. This guide concerns advanced disease that cannot be removed completely by surgery or has spread; it does not describe a postoperative recurrence-prevention course.

items.title: The tumour test
items.text: A BRAF V600 test helps identify whether BRAF-targeted medicines are an option. A tumour mutation does not by itself mean an inherited family condition. Keep the exact result and ask how it changes your choices.

items.title: Scans and local treatments
items.text: Record the scans used to follow known disease. Surgery or radiotherapy may have a separate role for a particular site; ask for their timing and risks to be added to the overall plan.

items.title: New changes still matter
items.text: Report a new lump, changing mole, persistent skin sore or unexplained symptom. A response at one site does not establish that every other symptom is harmless.

chapters.title: Your medicines and overall plan

chapters.title: Taking or receiving treatment safely
chapters.intro: Keep the written prescription and actual treatment record together.

items.title: Administration
items.text: The usual starting dose is 150 mg twice daily, about 12 hours apart. Take capsules at least one hour before or at least two hours after food. Swallow whole with water. Use the prescribed strength and dose, and check the label again after any interruption or dose change.

If you vomit after a dose, do not take a replacement dose; take the next dose when due. The team must give instructions for restarting after fever or another treatment hold.

items.title: Other medicines
items.text: Give the team a complete list of prescribed, over-the-counter and herbal medicines, supplements and allergies. Ask before adding a new medicine; treatment interactions and symptom-masking can matter.

items.title: Practical arrangements
items.text: Know where and when bloods are taken, how results reach the prescriber, and how to obtain the next supply or appointment. Ask for written instructions in a format you can use without a phone.

chapters.title: Tests, results and treatment decisions
chapters.intro: Safety tests and scans answer different questions.

items.title: Before treatment
items.text: Confirm BRAF V600 and check blood count, kidney and liver function, ECG, medicines and skin. Record existing skin lesions and relevant head-and-neck or other cancer assessments so later changes can be compared.

items.title: During treatment
items.text: Monthly blood count, kidney and liver tests, and monthly skin review. Repeat ECG when clinically indicated. NCCP also describes head-and-neck review every three months and other surveillance according to the individual assessment; this is separate from the cancer-response scan plan.

items.title: What a result means
items.text: Ask which result is abnormal, whether the finding needs a repeat test and whether treatment is held, changed or stopped. Do not use a reference range or one normal result to decide independently that a dose is safe.

items.title: Response and follow-up
items.text: Continue skin surveillance for up to six months after stopping, as specified by NCCP. Keep the agreed review for other new lesions and the individual response-imaging plan. No fixed tumour-marker schedule is assumed.

chapters.title: What to expect between visits
chapters.intro: A quiet treatment day does not rule out later problems.

items.title: Act on new symptoms
items.text: If your temperature is 38°C or higher, stop dabrafenib and contact the oncology team immediately under the current product information; do not restart on your own. Also call for shaking chills, dizziness, reduced urine, severe abdominal pain, eye pain or changed vision, or a blistering or spreading rash. Infection and medicine-related fever both need consideration.

items.title: Supportive medicines
items.text: NCCP classifies dabrafenib as minimal-to-low emetogenic risk; anti-sickness treatment follows local and individual need. Agree a written fever plan and keep a thermometer and actual urgent-contact number. items.title: A useful daily record
items.text: Record symptoms, temperature when unwell, bowel changes, fluid intake when reduced, missed doses and any medicines used for relief. Note how symptoms affect eating, walking, sleep and normal activities; this helps the team judge severity.

items.title: When life is affected
items.text: Tell the team about fatigue, pain, appetite, sleep, mood and ability to work or care for others. Practical and supportive care can accompany anticancer treatment; you do not have to wait until treatment ends.

chapters.title: Skin, body changes and daily care
chapters.intro: Use the detailed body map to locate symptoms, not to diagnose them.

items.title: Skin and sun
items.text: Inspect skin and report new lumps, persistent warty growths, sores or changing moles. Report painful thickening or redness of palms and soles before it limits walking or hand use. Protect skin from the sun and attend monthly skin reviews.

items.title: The body map
items.text: The organ anchors show possible locations and warning symptoms. They do not show how common each effect is, and a symptom may have another cause. New symptoms should be assessed in their clinical context.

items.title: Food, fluids and activity
items.text: Keep meals and fluids manageable and follow any individual fluid or diet restrictions. Gentle activity and rest can be adjusted to how you feel. Ask for dietetic or rehabilitation help if intake, weight, strength or mobility is falling.

items.title: Keep checking the plan
items.text: A new medicine, fever, hospital admission, procedure or radiotherapy may change treatment timing. Tell the oncology team and take the wallet card or medicine list to other appointments.

chapters.title: Fertility, pregnancy and breastfeeding
chapters.intro: Discuss these issues before the first dose whenever possible.

items.title: Contraception and pregnancy
items.text: Use effective contraception during dabrafenib alone and for two weeks after the last dose. Hormonal contraception may be less reliable; agree an effective alternative. A longer interval applies if another medicine requires it, so use your actual prescribed plan. Discuss fertility and breastfeeding before treatment.

items.title: Fertility preservation
items.text: Ask whether treatment or the cancer may affect fertility and whether fertility preservation is appropriate before treatment. A change in periods or sexual function does not reliably establish infertility.

items.title: Written dates and methods
items.text: Record the agreed method, last treatment date and how long precautions continue. Different medicines have different intervals, so ask for clarification after a switch or combination change.

items.title: Sexual health
items.text: Tell the team about sexual symptoms, relationship concerns or practical difficulties with the agreed precautions. Ask for a private discussion and specialist support when needed.

chapters.title: Decisions, support and useful records
chapters.intro: Your priorities belong in the treatment discussion.

items.title: Benefits and alternatives
items.text: Ask what the treatment aims to achieve, what alternatives are suitable, how likely important benefits are in your situation and how treatment burden or uncertainty affects that choice. A trial average cannot promise an individual outcome.

items.title: Support alongside treatment
items.text: Ask about symptom control, psychological support, finances, transport, work and help at home. Palliative or supportive care can be used alongside anticancer treatment to improve comfort and function.

items.title: A person you trust
items.text: If helpful, bring a family member or supporter and agree what information may be shared. Ask for an interpreter or accessible information when needed; use teach-back to check the schedule and urgent plan.

items.title: Your document set
items.text: Keep consent information, the three-page summary, complete handbook, treatment card, test plan and real contact details together. The QR opens more information but essential instructions remain available in print.

chapters.title: After a treatment hold, change or completion
chapters.intro: The next step should be written down, not assumed.

items.title: Follow-up and late effects
items.text: Continue skin surveillance for up to six months after stopping, as specified by NCCP. Keep the agreed review for other new lesions and the individual response-imaging plan. No fixed tumour-marker schedule is assumed.

items.title: Restarting or changing treatment
items.text: Skip a missed dose if the next dose is due in less than six hours. Do not take two doses together to make up for it. If you vomit after a dose, do not take a replacement dose; take the next dose when due. The team must give instructions for restarting after fever or another treatment hold.

items.title: A treatment summary
items.text: Record medicines and doses received, important side effects, admissions, last-dose date, ongoing symptom treatment and the clinician responsible for follow-up. Ask for an updated paper copy for your GP and other treating teams.

items.title: Your next review
items.text: Confirm the next blood test, scan and review, who explains the result, and which symptoms should trigger contact sooner. Keep actual daytime and out-of-hours numbers accessible after treatment stops.

questions.a: Yes. The complete handbook, three-page summary and cut-out wallet card are printable. Ask the team to enter actual contact numbers and provide an updated paper plan when anything changes.
